The book known in English as the Tibetan Book of the Dead is, in Tibetan, the Bardo Thödröl: Liberation through Hearing in the Between. It is read aloud to a dying person and, for days afterwards, to the dead, to tell them what they are seeing and how to be freed by recognising it. Tibetan tradition holds that Padmasambhava composed it in the eighth century and hid it, and that Karma Lingpa found it in the fourteenth. This first part is the book's own preface. It says for whom the book is meant, when and by whom it should be read, which prayers come first, and how the reader should sit and speak. It lays out the three stages that the rest of the book follows, and it ends with the first words spoken into the dying person's ear. Tibetan is written without spaces between words, and its spelling is far older than its pronunciation. Here the words are set apart, and a switch above the text shows under them either the letters as written or the word as it is said.
